title: Vows, Valuations, and What Belongs to God
summary: The book closes with rules for vows. A person vowed to the LORD could be released by paying a set value according to age and sex, with allowance for the poor. Animals, houses, and fields dedicated to God could be redeemed by paying their value plus a fifth. Firstborn animals and tithes already belong to God and cannot be vowed, and anything devoted to God by a ban can be neither sold nor redeemed.
story: Leviticus 26 ended with a formal conclusion, naming the laws God gave through Moses on Mount Sinai. Chapter 27 follows as an appendix, with its own closing line (verse 34). After the high drama of blessings and curses, the book ends on a quieter note: what happens when an ordinary Israelite, moved by gratitude or need, promises something to God. Placing vows here fits: chapter 26 dealt with the covenant God made with Israel, and chapter 27 deals with the voluntary promises Israelites made to God in response. The chapter draws on laws from earlier in the book, especially the Jubilee of chapter 25, and closes Leviticus by insisting that whatever is given to God must be treated as his.
historical:
Vows were a common part of ancient religion. A worshiper in trouble would promise a god a gift if the prayer was answered, and vows appear throughout the Old Testament. Jacob vowed to give God a tenth of everything if God brought him home safely (Genesis 28:20-22). Hannah vowed to give her son to the LORD if she conceived (1 Samuel 1:11), and Samuel served at the sanctuary as a result. Jephthah made a rash vow with tragic consequences (Judges 11). The wisdom writers warned that it was better not to vow at all than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:5). By the time of Jesus, some had turned vows into a way of escaping obligations: declaring property Corban, dedicated to God, so that it could not be used to support one's parents (Mark 7:11-13).

The values in verses 3 to 7 are in silver shekels, weighed rather than minted, since coins came into use in Israel's region only in the Persian period. The sanctuary shekel of twenty gerahs (verse 25) was a standard weight kept for temple payments. These were large sums for an ordinary family. For comparison, Joseph's brothers sold him for twenty shekels (Genesis 37:28), the value this chapter sets for a male between five and twenty years old. As with the rest of Leviticus, traditional readers date these laws to Sinai, while many critical scholars regard the chapter as a late addition to the book.
cultural:
When someone vowed a person to the LORD (often himself or a child), that person could not actually serve at the sanctuary; only Levites did that. Instead, the vow was fulfilled by paying the person's value to the sanctuary. The values vary with age and sex, and most interpreters connect them to the typical capacity for work in an agricultural economy: a man in his prime was valued most, children and the elderly less. The poor were not shut out of making vows: the priest could set a lower price according to what they could afford (verse 8).

The chapter distinguishes several kinds of holy things. An animal fit for sacrifice, once vowed, could not be swapped for another; if someone tried, both became holy. Unclean animals, houses, and fields could be redeemed at their value plus a fifth, a penalty that discouraged casual vowing and redeeming. Firstborn animals and tithes already belonged to God and could not be vowed as if they were gifts. The most serious category was cherem, what was devoted to God by a ban. It could not be redeemed at all. Verse 29 applies this to a person, most likely someone condemned to death under the law or in the wars of conquest, whose sentence could not be bought off. The tenth animal was chosen as the flock passed under the shepherd's staff, one by one, without inspecting whether it was good or bad, so that the owner could not keep the best for himself.
literary: The chapter is a practical law code organized by what is vowed: persons (verses 2 to 8), animals (verses 9 to 13), houses (verses 14 and 15), and fields (verses 16 to 25). It then turns to things that cannot be vowed because they already belong to God or are irrevocably devoted: firstborn animals (verses 26 and 27), devoted things (verses 28 and 29), and tithes (verses 30 to 33). Its most repeated terms are valuation, which appears twenty-one times, and holy. The phrase add a fifth recurs, as does the Jubilee, tying these rules to the land laws of chapter 25. The final verse echoes the end of chapter 26 and frames all of Leviticus as commandments given "on Mount Sinai".

outline.t: Vows involving persons and their valuation
Firstborn animals belong to the LORD
Things devoted to the LORD cannot be redeemed
Tithes, and the close of the book

doctrines.note: What is given to God becomes holy and cannot be quietly taken back or swapped for something worse. The chapter treats promises to God as serious, and it guards the difference between what is God's and what is ours.
The chapter's language of redemption, buying back what has been dedicated by paying a price, is the same vocabulary the Bible uses for God's rescue of his people. Redemption always costs something.
Firstborn animals and tithes belong to the LORD before anyone vows them. Giving them back acknowledges that the whole flock and harvest came from God in the first place.

words.note: Erekh, valuation or assessed value. It appears twenty-one times in this chapter and is its key word. It refers to the price set for redeeming a vowed person or thing, not to the person's worth before God. The same word is used for the value of a guilt offering in Leviticus 5.

Neder, a vow: a solemn promise to give something to God, often in exchange for an answered prayer. Vows were voluntary, but once made they were binding. This chapter makes vowing possible for rich and poor alike while ensuring that promises were kept.

Cherem, something devoted to God by a ban, set apart so completely that it can no longer be used by people. It could be given to the sanctuary (verse 28) or, in war and judgment, destroyed. The same root describes the destruction of Jericho in Joshua 6. It is the most absolute category of holiness in the chapter.

Ma'aser, a tithe or tenth. Tithes of crops and animals belonged to the LORD and supported the Levites and priests (Numbers 18) and, according to Deuteronomy 14, festival meals and the poor. Tithing predated the law: Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek in Genesis 14.

christ: Jesus spoke directly to abuses of vows and tithes. He condemned those who declared their property Corban to avoid supporting their parents, saying, "Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down" (Mark 7:13). He rebuked those who tithed "mint, dill, and cumin" while neglecting "justice, mercy, and faithfulness" (Matthew 23:23), without dismissing the tithe itself. The chapter's theme of redemption by payment takes on its deepest meaning in the New Testament: Paul tells believers, "You are not your own; you were bought at a price" (1 Corinthians 6:19-20), and Peter says they were redeemed "not with perishable things such as silver or gold" but "with the precious blood of Christ" (1 Peter 1:18-19). Where Leviticus priced the redemption of a vowed person in shekels, the New Testament says the redemption of people was paid with a life. And where a vowed person could only be dedicated by proxy, Paul calls believers to offer their whole selves to God (Romans 12:1).

hard.q: Why does the chapter value men more highly than women, and adults more than children and the elderly?
hard.a: The different values in verses 3 to 7 can look like a ranking of human worth, and modern readers are right to ask. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, understand them as reflecting the expected labor value of a person in an agricultural economy, the amount a vowed person's service would have been worth to the sanctuary, rather than their value before God. That is why the prime working years are valued most, and why a man past sixty is valued at less than a woman in her working years. Others note that the figures still reflect a patriarchal society in which women's work was undervalued, and that the text records those economic realities without endorsing them as God's view of persons. Both points can be true. The rest of Scripture is clear that every human being bears God's image (Genesis 1:27), and the New Testament declares that in Christ "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female" (Galatians 3:28). Verse 8 also ensures that the poor were never priced out of devotion: the priest adjusted the value to what they could afford.

questions: The chapter treats promises made to God as binding. Are there promises you have made to God, or to others before God, that you have quietly let slip?
An animal vowed to God could not be swapped for a worse one. Where are you tempted to give God something less than what you first offered?
Firstborn animals and tithes already belonged to God before anyone gave them. How would seeing everything you have as already his change the way you give?
